title: Channel-selective magnetic filtering in a nodal-line semimetal
authors: Hironmoy Pratihar, Alessandro De Martino, Arijit Kundu
abstract: We study quantum transport through a magnetic barrier in a nodal-line semimetal. When the Fermi energy lies near the nodal ring, the Fermi surface has toroidal geometry. Each cross-section in a plane parallel to the nodal ring consists of two concentric contours, inner and outer, carrying distinct transport channels. We show that a magnetic barrier resolves these two channels: because the contours enclose different momentum-space areas, they accommodate the field-induced transverse-momentum shift unequally, and the inner channel is cut off at a weaker barrier strength than the outer. Using a two-band effective Hamiltonian and a wave-function matching approach, we obtain closed-form, channel-resolved transmission amplitudes. Over a finite window of barrier strength the inner contour is fully blocked while the outer still transmits, so the barrier acts as a channel-selective filter. This sequential quenching shapes the two-terminal conductance, which decreases with barrier strength as the two channels close in turn and terminates once the outer channel is cut off, providing experimentally accessible fingerprints of the toroidal Fermi surface of a nodal-line semimetal.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes quantum transport in a nodal-line semimetal subjected to a magnetic barrier. By modeling the toroidal Fermi surface, the authors show that the barrier selectively filters the two distinct transport channels (inner and outer) at different critical strengths. This sequential quenching of conductance provides a unique, measurable signature confirming the material's underlying topological electronic structure.
main_problem: The study investigates quantum transport through a magnetic barrier in a nodal-line semimetal (NLS) to demonstrate a phenomenon called channel-selective magnetic filtering.
main_result: The magnetic barrier acts as a filter by sequentially blocking the inner and outer transport channels of the toroidal Fermi surface at different critical barrier strengths. This sequential quenching provides an experimental fingerprint of the NLS's toroidal geometry.
method: The authors employed a wave-function matching approach using a two-band effective Hamiltonian to derive closed-form, channel-resolved transmission amplitudes across the barrier.
model_or_system: The system is an NLS characterized by a nodal ring, leading to a toroidal constant-energy surface with two distinct inner and outer propagating channels. The transport is modeled by introducing a magnetic barrier (stripe) using a Landau gauge vector potential.
key_observables: Two-terminal conductance ($G/A$), channel-resolved transmission amplitudes ($|t_s|^2$), and the dependence of conductance on barrier strength ($BL$) and Fermi energy ($E$).
important_parameters: The field-width product ($BL$), the Fermi energy ($E$), and the characteristic momentum scale ($q_0$).
main_assumptions: The magnetic barrier is idealized as a step profile (uniform $B$ over width $L$), and the analysis assumes the film thickness is much smaller than the fringe field decay length.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the NLS magnetic-barrier geometry, the constant-energy surface cross-sections showing two channels, and plots demonstrating the asymmetric suppression of the two channels' transmission probabilities and the total conductance as the barrier strength increases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (NLS with toroidal FS) and the transport setup (magnetic barrier). It then applies the Hamiltonian and wave-function matching techniques to derive channel-resolved transmission. The core argument builds by showing the unequal response of the inner and outer channels to the magnetic field, culminating in the prediction of sequential conductance quenching.
why_interesting: The concept of channel-selective filtering based on the topology of the Fermi surface is a sophisticated manifestation of quantum transport physics, relevant to understanding topological materials and their response to external fields.
